<reflection>
- The second experiment (low substrate, high catalyst, high product) successfully shifted the NLL values, but the top 15 models remain extremely tightly clustered (NLLs between -39.5 and -40.5). 
- This indicates that the models still have enough parametric flexibility to fit both the baseline and the high-catalyst/high-product regimes equally well. Specifically, models with substrate deactivation (M11), product deactivation (M12), simple catalyst decay (M9), and higher-order catalyst mechanisms (M5, M18) are all still highly plausible.
- My aim to break the degeneracy was only partially achieved; we need a condition that isolates these specific effects rather than mixing them. We must break the correlation between substrate, product, and catalyst concentration effects.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To cleanly separate the leading deactivation models (M11, M12, M9) from the higher-order catalyst models (M5, M18, M19), I propose an experiment at the opposite extreme: maximum substrate ([S]0 = 5.0), very low catalyst ([cat]0 = 0.01), and zero initial product ([P]0 = 0.0).
1. **Maximum Substrate ([S]0 = 5.0):** This will strongly drive substrate-induced deactivation (M11). Because the catalyst concentration is so low, if M11 is true, the catalyst will be completely deactivated very early in the reaction, leading to a premature plateau in product formation.
2. **Zero Initial Product ([P]0 = 0.0):** This completely turns off product-induced deactivation (M12) at the start of the reaction. If M12 is true, the reaction will start at maximum velocity and only slow down as product accumulates. This provides a stark contrast to M11 (which slows down immediately) and M9 (which slows down purely as a function of time).
3. **Very Low Catalyst ([cat]0 = 0.01):** This minimizes the rate of any second-order catalyst interactions (M5, M18, M19, M2). Under these conditions, those higher-order models will behave essentially identically to the simple Michaelis-Menten model (M1). 
By suppressing the higher-order catalyst effects and maximizing the divergence between the different deactivation triggers (S vs. P vs. time), this experiment will force the models to make distinct predictions about the shape of the reaction curve.
</hypothesis>
